name: RMS voltage
seoDesc: RMS voltage: work out RMS voltage (Voltage) from the RMS voltage. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The RMS voltage calculator is a free, no-sign-up physics tool. Fill in the 4 fields it asks for and it works out RMS voltage (Voltage) straight away, with the formula shown underneath. It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the RMS voltage calculator work?
sections.html:
The RMS voltage calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports RMS voltage (Voltage) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the waveform shape and the characteristic voltage); then you type in the RMS voltage (Voltage) and the RMS voltage (Voltage).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the RMS voltage calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

RMS voltage=(1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (2 × (voltage ^ 2) + 4 × (wave offset (V₀) ^ 2))
RMS voltage=(1 ÷ 4) × the square root of (2 × (voltage ^ 2) + 16 × (wave offset (V₀) ^ 2))
RMS voltage=(1 ÷ 4) × the square root of (2 × (PI ^ 2) × (voltage ^ 2) + 16 × (wave offset (V₀) ^ 2))
RMS voltage=the square root of ((voltage ^ 2) + (wave offset (V₀) ^ 2))
Wave offset (V₀)=(1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (-(voltage ^ 2) + 4 × (RMS voltage ^ 2))
Voltage=the square root of (-(wave offset (V₀) ^ 2) + (RMS voltage ^ 2))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Waveform shape set to Sine wave, Characteristic voltage set to Peak voltage (Vp), Voltage = 10 V and Wave offset (V₀) = 10 V. The calculator returns RMS voltage = 12.2474 V.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: RMS voltage = 12.2474 V should be roughly the size you expected from Waveform shape set to Sine wave and Characteristic voltage set to Peak voltage (Vp).

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The RMS voltage calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the RMS voltage — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the RMS voltage calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns RMS voltage (Voltage), derived from the RMS voltage. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the RMS voltage calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the RMS voltage, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter voltage in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Voltage opens in volts and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports RMS voltage = 12.2474 V. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the RMS voltage calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
